questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Physical Quantity) List II (SI Unit)
(A) Magnetic Field (\(B\)) (I) \(\text{A m}^2\)
(B) Magnetic Dipole Moment (\(m\)) (II) \(\text{T}\)
(C) Permeability of Free Space (\(\mu_0\)) (III) \(\text{N m rad}^{-1}\)
(D) Torsional Constant of Suspension Spring (\(k\)) (IV) \(\text{T m A}^{-1}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: SI Unit of Magnetic Field (\(B\))
The magnetic Lorentz force on a moving charge is given by \(F = q v B \sin\theta\). Solving for the magnetic field gives \(B = \frac{F}{q v \sin\theta}\). In SI units, this is \(\frac{\text{N}}{\text{C}\cdot\text{m s}^{-1}} = \frac{\text{N}}{\text{A}\cdot\text{m}}\), which is defined as the tesla (\(\text{T}\)). Therefore, Magnetic Field (\(B\)) corresponds to \(\text{T}\).

Step 2: SI Unit of Magnetic Dipole Moment (\(m\))
The magnetic dipole moment of a current-carrying planar coil of \(N\) turns and area \(A\) carrying current \(I\) is defined as \(m = N I A\). The SI unit of electric current is ampere (\(\text{A}\)) and that of area is square metre (\(\text{m}^2\)). Thus, the SI unit of magnetic dipole moment is \(\text{A m}^2\). Therefore, Magnetic Dipole Moment (\(m\)) corresponds to \(\text{A m}^2\).

Step 3: SI Unit of Permeability of Free Space (\(\mu_0\))
From Ampere's circuital law or the magnetic field around a straight conductor \(B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\), we obtain \(\mu_0 = \frac{2\pi r B}{I}\). Substituting the SI units gives \(\frac{\text{m}\cdot\text{T}}{\text{A}} = \text{T m A}^{-1}\) (equivalently \(\text{N A}^{-2}\)). Therefore, Permeability of Free Space (\(\mu_0\)) corresponds to \(\text{T m A}^{-1}\).

Step 4: SI Unit of Torsional Constant of Suspension Spring (\(k\))
In a moving coil galvanometer, the restoring torque exerted by the suspension spring or phosphor bronze strip is given by \(\tau = k \theta\), where \(\tau\) is the restoring torque and \(\theta\) is the angular deflection in radians. Thus, \(k = \frac{\tau}{\theta}\). The SI unit of torque is newton metre (\(\text{N m}\)) and that of angle is radian (\(\text{rad}\)), giving \(\text{N m rad}^{-1}\). Therefore, Torsional Constant (\(k\)) corresponds to \(\text{N m rad}^{-1}\).

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The correct correspondence between the physical quantities and their SI units is: Magnetic Field (\(B\)) pairs with (II), Magnetic Dipole Moment (\(m\)) pairs with (I), Permeability of Free Space (\(\mu_0\)) pairs with (IV), and Torsional Constant (\(k\)) pairs with (III). Hence, the correct combination is A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_MATCH_MCQ_Q02 - Magnetic field expressions for current configurations

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Current Distribution / Position) List II (Magnetic Field Magnitude)
(A) Centre of a flat circular loop of radius \(R\) carrying current \(I\) (I) \(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\)
(B) Distance \(r\) from a long straight wire carrying current \(I\) (II) \(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 R}\)
(C) Interior of a long ideal solenoid carrying current \(I\) with \(n\) turns per unit length (III) \(\dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2 x^3}\)
(D) Axis of a circular loop of radius \(R\) at large distance \(x \gg R\) (IV) \(\mu_0 n I\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Magnetic Field at the Centre of a Circular Loop
From the Biot-Savart law, the magnetic field at the centre of a flat single-turn circular loop of radius \(R\) carrying current \(I\) is obtained by integrating \(d B = \frac{\mu_0 I \, d l}{4\pi R^2}\) over the perimeter \(2\pi R\), yielding \(B = \frac{\mu_0 I (2\pi R)}{4\pi R^2} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2 R}\). Therefore, the centre of a flat circular loop corresponds to \(\frac{\mu_0 I}{2 R}\).

Step 2: Magnetic Field of a Long Straight Current-Carrying Wire
Applying Ampere's circuital law along a concentric circular path of radius \(r\) perpendicular to a long straight wire carrying current \(I\), we have \(\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I\). Solving for \(B\) gives \(B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\). Therefore, the distance \(r\) from a long straight wire corresponds to \(\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\).

Step 3: Magnetic Field Inside a Long Ideal Solenoid
Applying Ampere's circuital law to a rectangular loop enclosing \(n h\) turns of a long ideal solenoid carrying current \(I\), the field outside is negligible and along the axis it is uniform: \(B h = \mu_0 (n h I)\), which yields \(B = \mu_0 n I\). Therefore, the interior of a long ideal solenoid corresponds to \(\mu_0 n I\).

Step 4: Magnetic Field on the Axis of a Circular Loop at Large Distance
The axial magnetic field of a circular current loop of radius \(R\) at an axial distance \(x\) from the centre is given by \(B = \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}\). For points far away along the axis such that \(x \gg R\), this expression simplifies to \(B \approx \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2 x^3}\). Therefore, the axis of a circular loop at large distance corresponds to \(\frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2 x^3}\).

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The correct correspondence between current configurations and their magnetic fields is: The centre of a circular loop pairs with (II), the straight wire pairs with (I), the interior of a solenoid pairs with (IV), and the distant axial point of a loop pairs with (III). Hence, the correct combination is A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_MATCH_MCQ_Q03 - Charged particle motion in magnetic and electric fields

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Motion / Device Parameter) List II (Governing Mathematical Expression)
(A) Cyclotron angular frequency (\(\omega_c\)) (I) \(\dfrac{E}{B}\)
(B) Pitch of helical trajectory (\(p\)) (II) \(\dfrac{2\pi m v_\parallel}{q B}\)
(C) Condition for undeflected motion in crossed fields (\(v\)) (III) \(\dfrac{q B}{m}\)
(D) Radius of circular trajectory in uniform \(B\) (\(r\)) (IV) \(\dfrac{m v_\perp}{q B}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Cyclotron Angular Frequency (\(\omega_c\))
When a charged particle of mass \(m\) and charge \(q\) moves in a circular path perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field \(B\), the magnetic Lorentz force provides the necessary centripetal force: \(\frac{m v^2}{r} = q v B\). Since the linear speed is related to angular frequency by \(v = \omega_c r\), substituting gives \(m \omega_c^2 r = q (\omega_c r) B\), which simplifies to \(\omega_c = \frac{q B}{m}\). Therefore, Cyclotron angular frequency corresponds to \(\frac{q B}{m}\).

Step 2: Pitch of Helical Trajectory (\(p\))
When the velocity vector of a charged particle makes an arbitrary angle with the uniform magnetic field, the velocity resolves into a parallel component \(v_\parallel\) and a perpendicular component \(v_\perp\). The period of circular revolution in the plane perpendicular to the field is \(T = \frac{2\pi r}{v_\perp} = \frac{2\pi m}{q B}\). The pitch \(p\) is the linear distance traversed along the magnetic field during one complete revolution: \(p = v_\parallel T = v_\parallel \left(\frac{2\pi m}{q B}\right) = \frac{2\pi m v_\parallel}{q B}\). Therefore, Pitch of helical trajectory corresponds to \(\frac{2\pi m v_\parallel}{q B}\).

Step 3: Condition for Undeflected Motion in Crossed Fields (\(v\))
In a velocity selector with mutually perpendicular electric field \(\vec{E}\) and magnetic field \(\vec{B}\), the electric force is \(\vec{F}_e = q \vec{E}\) and the magnetic force is \(\vec{F}_m = q (\vec{v} \times \vec{B})\). For the particle to pass undeflected, the net Lorentz force must be zero: \(\vec{F}_e + \vec{F}_m = 0\), which requires their magnitudes to balance: \(q E = q v B\), giving \(v = \frac{E}{B}\). Therefore, Condition for undeflected motion in crossed fields corresponds to \(\frac{E}{B}\).

Step 4: Radius of Circular Trajectory (\(r\))
The perpendicular velocity component \(v_\perp\) causes circular motion in the transverse plane where the magnetic force acts as centripetal force: \(\frac{m v_\perp^2}{r} = q v_\perp B\). Solving for the radius of orbit gives \(r = \frac{m v_\perp}{q B}\). Therefore, Radius of circular trajectory corresponds to \(\frac{m v_\perp}{q B}\).

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The correct correspondence between the dynamical parameters and expressions is: Cyclotron angular frequency pairs with (III), Pitch of helical trajectory pairs with (II), Undeflected motion condition pairs with (I), and Radius of circular trajectory pairs with (IV). Hence, the correct combination is A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_MATCH_MCQ_Q04 - Moving coil galvanometer parameters and circuit conversions

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Galvanometer Parameter / Conversion) List II (Mathematical Expression)
(A) Current Sensitivity of Galvanometer (\(I_s\)) (I) \(\dfrac{N A B}{k R_g}\)
(B) Voltage Sensitivity of Galvanometer (\(V_s\)) (II) \(\dfrac{I_g R_g}{I - I_g}\)
(C) Shunt resistance (\(S\)) to convert into an ammeter of range \(I\) (III) \(\dfrac{N A B}{k}\)
(D) Series resistance (\(R\)) to convert into a voltmeter of range \(V\) (IV) \(\dfrac{V}{I_g} - R_g\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Current Sensitivity of Galvanometer (\(I_s\))
In a moving coil galvanometer with radial magnetic field, the deflecting magnetic torque is \(\tau = N I A B\) and the restoring torque is \(\tau = k \theta\). In equilibrium, \(k \theta = N I A B\), which gives the angular deflection per unit current as \(I_s = \frac{\theta}{I} = \frac{N A B}{k}\). Therefore, Current Sensitivity corresponds to \(\frac{N A B}{k}\).

Step 2: Voltage Sensitivity of Galvanometer (\(V_s\))
The voltage sensitivity is defined as the deflection produced per unit applied voltage: \(V_s = \frac{\theta}{V} = \frac{\theta}{I R_g}\), where \(R_g\) is the resistance of the galvanometer coil. Substituting \(\frac{\theta}{I} = \frac{N A B}{k}\) yields \(V_s = \frac{N A B}{k R_g}\). Therefore, Voltage Sensitivity corresponds to \(\frac{N A B}{k R_g}\).

Step 3: Shunt Resistance for Ammeter Conversion (\(S\))
To convert a galvanometer of internal resistance \(R_g\) and full-scale deflection current \(I_g\) into an ammeter measuring up to total current \(I\), a low shunt resistance \(S\) is connected in parallel with the coil. Since both branches share the same potential difference, \(I_g R_g = (I - I_g) S\). Solving for the shunt resistance gives \(S = \frac{I_g R_g}{I - I_g}\). Therefore, Shunt resistance corresponds to \(\frac{I_g R_g}{I - I_g}\).

Step 4: Series Resistance for Voltmeter Conversion (\(R\))
To convert the galvanometer into a voltmeter capable of reading a potential difference up to \(V\), a large resistance \(R\) is connected in series with the coil. The total potential difference across the combination when full-scale current \(I_g\) flows is \(V = I_g (R_g + R)\). Solving for the series resistance gives \(R_g + R = \frac{V}{I_g}\), hence \(R = \frac{V}{I_g} - R_g\). Therefore, Series resistance corresponds to \(\frac{V}{I_g} - R_g\).

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The correct correspondence between the galvanometer metrics and their expressions is: Current Sensitivity pairs with (III), Voltage Sensitivity pairs with (I), Shunt resistance pairs with (II), and Series resistance pairs with (IV). Hence, the correct combination is A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV.
